title: Delivery Time Estimate
statement: A delivery app has a road graph of 200,000 intersections and 500,000 roads with travel times in seconds. For each new order it needs the fastest time from the restaurant to the customer.
examples: Small map: 3 roads of 5 s beat 1 road of 60 s

approaches.name: Dijkstra with a binary heap
approaches.label: best
approaches.why: About 10⁷ steps; exact with positive times.

approaches.name: Bellman–Ford
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: 10¹¹ steps: far too slow when no edge is negative.

approaches.name: BFS on road count
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: Fast but wrong: ignores travel times.

approaches.name: A* with straight-line distance as a guide
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Same answer and usually faster for one destination; needs coordinates.

title: Build Pipeline Order
statement: A monorepo has 8,000 packages and 20,000 "depends on" links. The CI system must find an order to build every package after its dependencies, or report a cycle.
examples: app → lib → utils gives utils, lib, app

approaches.name: Kahn's algorithm (queue of packages with no unbuilt dependencies)
approaches.label: best
approaches.why: Linear, gives the order, and reports a cycle when packages are left.

approaches.name: DFS post-order with a three-colour cycle check
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Same bound; recursion depth needs care on long chains.

approaches.name: Sort packages by number of dependencies
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: Wrong: a package with one dependency can still need many others first.

approaches.name: Try to build everything, retry the failures until nothing changes
approaches.label: unsuitable

title: Budget Flight Search
statement: A travel site has 300 airports and 20,000 one-way fares. A customer wants the cheapest trip from one airport to another with at most 3 stopovers.
examples: Direct 500, or 2 flights for 200: with 1 stopover allowed → 200

approaches.name: Bellman–Ford for k + 1 rounds, each from a copy of the last
approaches.label: best
approaches.why: 8 × 10⁴ relaxations, exact with the stop limit.

approaches.name: Dijkstra on (airport, flights used) states
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Correct; more code than needed for a small k.

approaches.name: Plain Dijkstra on price
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: Ignores the stop limit; the cheapest trip may use too many flights.

approaches.name: List every trip of up to 4 flights
approaches.label: unsuitable
